description: We’re a multidisciplinary team united by curiosity and a passion for science and technology. We bring together software development, UI/UX and graphic design, data analysis, research, and creative thinking. At the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we combine our skills and perspectives to turn ideas into practical, user-friendly solutions that use space technology and Earth observation to tackle real-world challenges.
summary:
Every autumn, Uzbekistan's farmers decide what to plant on shrinking irrigation water and tiring soil. We built project FarmLab that turns NASA data combined with Local and other International public data into a decision helping tool.

A farmer taps their field and answers three questions; NASA MODIS greenness already suggests what grew there. FarmLab then grows all 14 local crops, on paper, through 25 years of NASA POWER weather shifted to likely 2026–2030 conditions, with GRACE ground-water trends and live SMAP soil moisture and GPM rain. It returns three 3-year rotations beside the farmer's own, each showing why it was chosen, water, income and soil against today, pros, risks, a calendar of bare and heat-stressed months, the evidence and data gaps behind every number, and a checklist for the local agronomist. 
Advanced Customization helps farmer's specific conditions. The advice is checked, not guessed: water use is calibrated to the challenge's irrigation data, climate bands are back-tested, and picks match local farming practice in all 13 regions. It works in Uzbek, Russian and English, with no account. FarmLab helps farmers rebuild soil health, save water, and keep income as Central Asia's climate shifts.
details:
What It Does and How It Works

FarmLab helps farmers compare what to plant next and plan crop rotations over three years. Farmers can select a region or pin a field, enter recent crops and available irrigation water, and choose a priority such as saving water, improving soil, or increasing income. FarmLab tests crops against historical and projected growing conditions, then presents three rotation plans.

The project combines NASA POWER weather data with crop water requirements to estimate rainfall, heat, frost, and irrigation needs. It also uses NASA GRACE water storage, MODIS crop-season observations, SoilGrids soil carbon, regional salinity, and crop yield and price data from Uzbek and international sources. An interactive diagram on the landing page shows how these sources feed into FarmLab’s calculations and recommendations.

Benefits and Intended Impact

FarmLab makes complex climate and agricultural data easier to use in everyday planning. It aims to help farmers choose crops suited to local climate and water supplies, plan more diverse rotations, and compare tradeoffs among water use, soil health, and gross income. Over time, better-informed decisions could support more resilient farms and more sustainable water use.

Tools and Technologies

FarmLab is built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. Python scripts prepare regional data. The project uses NASA datasets and open agricultural data, presented through a responsive web interface with interactive maps, charts, and SVG diagrams. Farmers can use it in a web browser, and saved field settings stay in the browser without an account.

What Makes It Creative

FarmLab turns climate and agricultural data into three practical crop rotation plans. Farmers can compare plans for different goals, then use Advanced customization to adjust how recommendations are scored and tailor them to their field. The interactive data flow also makes the sources and calculations behind each recommendation visible.

Factors the Team Considered

The project accounts for local growing seasons, irrigation limits, heat and frost risk, crop rotation, salinity, soil condition, crop prices, and which crops are commonly grown in each region. The team also considered phone usability, multiple languages, and uncertainty in the data. Income is shown as gross income because reliable cost data is not available. FarmLab is intended to support—not replace—local agronomists.
